etymology: Jacob (Hebrew Ya'aqov) means "he grasps the heel" or "he supplants"; Laban (Hebrew Lavan) means "white," the Aramean kinsman of Rebekah dwelling in Padan-aram.
biblical_def: When Jacob fled from the wrath of Esau, the LORD sent him to Padan-aram, to the house of Laban his mother's brother, and there the patriarch labored fourteen years for Rachel and Leah and six more for his flocks. The narrative of Genesis 29 through 31 is a true history in which the supplanter is himself supplanted: Jacob who had deceived his father is deceived by Laban, who substituted Leah for Rachel under cover of the wedding night, exacting a second seven years of service. Yet through all of Laban's grasping—changing Jacob's wages ten times—the sovereign hand of God prospered His chosen heir, multiplying the ringstraked and speckled cattle so that the man increased exceedingly. Here is providence vindicated: the LORD turns the craft of the deceitful to bless His covenant servant, fulfilling the promise made at Bethel. The twelve tribes of Israel were begotten in these years, and the household idols Rachel stole testify to the lingering darkness from which grace would purge the nation. At Mizpah the two men raised a heap of stones and a covenant of separation, the LORD set as watchman between them. The whole account preaches that no schemer's deceit can frustrate the eternal purpose, and that God disciplines His own even while He keeps them.
webster_summary: The account of Jacob's twenty years of service in the house of his uncle Laban, where he won his wives and his flocks under repeated deceit.
webster_full: JACOB AND LABAN, proper nouns. Jacob, "he that supplanteth"; Laban, "white," the Syrian father of Leah and Rachel.
The patriarch's sojourn in Padan-aram, recorded in Genesis chapters twenty-nine through thirty-one.
A pattern of mutual contention in which the deceiver Jacob meets a craftier deceiver in his kinsman.
As it is written, "And Jacob served seven years for Rachel; and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her" (Gen 29:20).
A standing witness that the providence of God prospers His elect through the very wrongs of wicked men.
scriptures: And Jacob served seven years for Rachel; and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her.
And it came to pass, that in the morning, behold, it was Leah: and he said to Laban, What is this thou hast done unto me? did not I serve with thee for Rachel? wherefore then hast thou beguiled me?
Gen 31:7
And your father hath deceived me, and changed my wages ten times; but God suffered him not to hurt me.

Except the God of my father, the God of Abraham, and the fear of Isaac, had been with me, surely thou hadst sent me away now empty. God hath seen mine affliction and the labour of my hands, and rebuked thee yesternight.
corruption_summary: This account faces little direct postmodern redefinition, though its plain endorsement of patriarchal household order and God's favor toward His covenant line is quietly resisted.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The biblical principle to recover is the doctrine of particular providence: that the LORD governs every circumstance, even the wages changed ten times and the deceit of an unbelieving kinsman, to accomplish His covenant promise. Jacob did not prosper by his own cunning with the rods and the watering troughs but because, as he confessed, the God of his fathers had been with him.

A faithful reading also recovers the seriousness of deception as sin. Jacob who supplanted his brother and beguiled his father reaps in Laban's house the same measure he had meted out. Scripture does not gloss the patriarch's faults nor Laban's greed; it shows a holy God disciplining His own while keeping His word, that we might learn the fear of the LORD and the comfort of His unfailing election.
roots_summary: The episode is rooted in the Abrahamic covenant carried forward through Isaac to Jacob, the chosen heir of the promise.
roots_lines: The flight to Padan-aram followed Jacob's deceit of Isaac and the stolen blessing (Gen 27-28).
At Bethel the LORD had pledged to keep Jacob and bring him again to the land (Gen 28:15).
The twelve sons born of Leah, Rachel, Bilhah, and Zilpah became the tribes of Israel.
Laban's pursuit and the Mizpah covenant closed the sojourn with a heap of witness (Gen 31:48-49).
The wrestling at Peniel that followed sealed the new name Israel upon the returning patriarch (Gen 32).
usage: Jacob's seven years that seemed but a few days are cited as an emblem of love's patience.
The phrase "God suffered him not to hurt me" is a watchword of trust in providence.
The Mizpah benediction is often quoted, though its original sense was a covenant of wary separation.

etymology: Sarah (Hebrew Sarah) means "princess," the freeborn wife of Abraham; Hagar (Hebrew Hagar) was her Egyptian bondwoman, whose name is linked to wandering or flight.
biblical_def: Sarah the freewoman and Hagar the bondwoman stand together in the history of Genesis 16 and 21 as the two mothers of Abraham's house, and the apostle Paul declares them an allegory of the two covenants. When the promised seed delayed, Sarah gave her Egyptian handmaid to Abraham, and Hagar conceived Ishmael after the flesh by the strength of nature and the impatience of unbelief. But the LORD had promised a son by Sarah, and in due time Isaac was born after the Spirit, the child of promise, when both parents were as good as dead. The mocking of the bondwoman's son against the heir of promise brought the casting out of Hagar and Ishmael, which Paul in Galatians 4 sets forth as a type: Hagar answers to Mount Sinai, the covenant of bondage and works, gendering to bondage with her children; Sarah answers to the Jerusalem which is above, the mother of the free, the covenant of grace whose children are born by promise. So the believer learns he is not a child of the bondwoman but of the free, justified not by the works of the law but by faith in the promised Seed. Yet the LORD heard the cry of the lad and showed mercy even to Hagar in the wilderness, for He is gracious.
webster_summary: Abraham's wife and her Egyptian bondwoman, whom the apostle expounds as a figure of the two covenants of bondage and of grace.
webster_full: SARAH AND HAGAR, proper nouns. Sarah, "princess," the freewoman; Hagar, the Egyptian bondwoman of Abraham's household.
The two mothers whose sons, Isaac and Ishmael, divide the line of the flesh from the line of promise.
In Paul's allegory, a figure of Sinai in bondage and of the heavenly Jerusalem in freedom (Gal 4).
As it is written, "Cast out the bondwoman and her son: for the son of the bondwoman shall not be heir with the son of the freewoman" (Gen 21:10).
A type teaching justification by promise and faith, not by the works of the law.
scriptures: And Hagar bare Abram a son: and Abram called his son's name, which Hagar bare, Ishmael.
Gen 21:2
For Sarah conceived, and bare Abraham a son in his old age, at the set time of which God had spoken to him.
Wherefore she said unto Abraham, Cast out this bondwoman and her son: for the son of this bondwoman shall not be heir with my son, even with Isaac.
Gal 4:31
So then, brethren, we are not children of the bondwoman, but of the free.
corruption_summary: Modern readings sometimes recast Sarah as oppressor and Hagar merely as victim, eclipsing the covenantal typology the apostle himself draws.
corruption_paragraphs: Where the Spirit through Paul gives us an allegory of bondage and freedom, of law and grace, contemporary retellings often flatten the account into a story of social grievance, casting Hagar simply as the wronged outsider and Sarah as the privileged abuser. This inverts the inspired interpretation. Genesis does record Sarah's harshness and Hagar's affliction without excusing them, and it shows the tender mercy of the LORD who hears the bondwoman's cry; but the canonical point is not a parable of victimhood.

The principle to recover is the apostolic typology itself. Hagar and Sinai gender to bondage; the works of the law cannot bring forth the heir. Sarah and the Jerusalem above gender to freedom; the child of promise is born by grace through faith. To read the narrative aright is to find in it the very gospel of justification, and to rejoice that we are children not of the bondwoman but of the free.
roots_summary: The account is rooted in the promise of a seed to Abraham and its fulfillment against the impatience of the flesh.
roots_lines: The covenant of Genesis 15 promised Abraham a son from his own body.
Hagar's son Ishmael was conceived by human contrivance when faith faltered (Gen 16).
Isaac, the child of promise, was born at the set time God had appointed (Gen 21:2).
Paul interprets the two women as the two covenants in Galatians 4:22-31.
The casting out of the bondwoman prefigures that law and grace cannot share the inheritance.
usage: "The bondwoman and the freewoman" is shorthand for the contrast of law and gospel.
Isaac as "the child of promise" names every believer born again by grace.
Hagar's well, Beer-lahai-roi, marks the place where God who sees showed mercy to the afflicted.

etymology: Jonathan (Hebrew Yehonathan) means "the LORD has given," the eldest son of King Saul; David (Hebrew Dawid) means "beloved," the son of Jesse anointed king over Israel.
biblical_def: Jonathan the son of Saul and David the son of Jesse are joined in Scripture as the pattern of covenant friendship, recorded in First Samuel chapters eighteen through twenty. When David had slain Goliath, the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and he loved him as his own soul; and Jonathan made a covenant with David, stripping himself of his robe and his garments, even his sword and his bow and his girdle, and giving them to the LORD's anointed. Here is self-denying love at its highest pitch among men, for Jonathan was heir to the throne, yet he willingly preferred the man God had chosen above himself, saying, Thou shalt be king over Israel, and I shall be next unto thee. He warned David of his father's murderous designs, interceded for him, and bound their houses in a covenant of loyalty before the LORD. This friendship was not mere natural affection but a bond sealed in the fear of God and in submission to the divine election of David. Jonathan's love, surpassing the love of women, dimly images the love of Christ who lays down His robes and His life for His friends, and the love that ought to bind the saints. Though Jonathan fell in battle, David kept the covenant to his seed in Mephibosheth, showing kindness for Jonathan's sake.
webster_summary: The covenant friendship of Saul's son and David, marked by a love that gladly yielded the throne to the LORD's anointed.
webster_full: JONATHAN AND DAVID, proper nouns. Jonathan, "the LORD has given"; David, "beloved," the anointed king.
The friendship recorded in First Samuel, sealed by a covenant and a token of garments.
A pattern of self-denying loyalty, the heir preferring the chosen above his own crown.
As it is written, "Then Jonathan and David made a covenant, because he loved him as his own soul" (1 Sam 18:3).
A faint image of the love of Christ for His friends and the love that binds the saints.
scriptures: And it came to pass, when he had made an end of speaking unto Saul, that the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.
Then Jonathan and David made a covenant, because he loved him as his own soul.
And Jonathan caused David to swear again, because he loved him: for he loved him as he loved his own soul.

And Jonathan said to David, Go in peace, forasmuch as we have sworn both of us in the name of the LORD, saying, The LORD be between me and thee, and between my seed and thy seed for ever. And he arose and departed: and Jonathan went into the city.
corruption_summary: Modern voices sometimes distort this covenant friendship into a romantic or sexual reading, against the plain witness of the text.
corruption_paragraphs: Recent attempts to sexualize the friendship of Jonathan and David impose an alien category upon a chaste and holy bond. The text speaks of a love knit in soul and sealed by covenant before the LORD, the love of brothers in arms and saints in faith. To recast it as an erotic relationship not only contradicts the express moral law of God, which everywhere condemns such union, but also robs Scripture of its true and higher meaning. David's lament that Jonathan's love was wonderful, passing the love of women, exalts the purity and depth of covenant loyalty, not carnal desire.

The principle to recover is the dignity of godly friendship and self-denying love. Jonathan, the natural heir, gladly subordinated his ambition to the revealed will of God, preferring David whom the LORD had chosen. Such love—willing to lay down its own glory for another and for the kingdom of God—points beyond itself to the love of the Lord Jesus, who emptied Himself and laid down His life for His friends.
roots_summary: The bond is rooted in submission to God's sovereign choice of David and in the covenant-keeping faith of both men.
roots_lines: David's anointing by Samuel set him apart as the LORD's chosen king (1 Sam 16).
Jonathan's love arose after David's victory over Goliath (1 Sam 18:1).
The covenant was renewed and bound to their seed for ever (1 Sam 20:42).
Saul's jealousy made Jonathan an intercessor and protector for David.
David kept the covenant after Jonathan's death by his kindness to Mephibosheth (2 Sam 9).
usage: "Knit in soul" describes the deepest godly friendship between believers.
Jonathan stripping off his robe pictures the surrender of self for the LORD's anointed.
The covenant "between my seed and thy seed" shows friendship binding even future generations.

etymology: Dinah (Hebrew Dinah) means "judgment" or "vindicated," from the root for judging; she was the daughter of Jacob by Leah.
biblical_def: Dinah, the daughter of Jacob and Leah, is the central figure of the grievous history in Genesis 34. When she went out to see the daughters of the land, Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite, prince of the country, saw her, took her, and defiled her, humbling her by force. Though his soul afterward clave to the maiden and he sought her in marriage, the wrong against the covenant household could not be undone. The narrative is a true and sober account of the corruption of the Canaanite nations and the perils that beset Israel when she mingles with the heathen. Jacob's sons Simeon and Levi, full brothers of Dinah, answered the defilement with treachery and slaughter, persuading the men of Shechem to be circumcised and then, while they were sore, falling upon the city and putting every male to the sword. Their deceitful cruelty Jacob rebuked, and on his deathbed he cursed their fierce anger, scattering them in Israel. The account holds forth at once the seriousness of sexual sin against the covenant people, the danger of unequal communion with the wicked, and the evil of avenging wrong by treachery and bloodshed. It teaches that vengeance belongs to the LORD, and that even within the chosen family sin abounds, awaiting the grace that would redeem.
webster_summary: The daughter of Jacob and Leah, defiled at Shechem, whose dishonor provoked the bloody and treacherous vengeance of her brothers.
webster_full: DINAH, proper noun. From the Hebrew for "judgment" or "vindication"; the daughter of Jacob by Leah.
The maiden whose defilement at Shechem is recorded in Genesis chapter thirty-four.
The occasion of Simeon and Levi's deceitful slaughter of the men of the city.
As it is written, "And Dinah the daughter of Leah, which she bare unto Jacob, went out to see the daughters of the land" (Gen 34:1).
A warning against mingling with the heathen and against avenging wrong by treachery.
scriptures: Gen 34:1
And Dinah the daughter of Leah, which she bare unto Jacob, went out to see the daughters of the land.
Gen 34:2
And when Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite, prince of the country, saw her, he took her, and lay with her, and defiled her.

And it came to pass on the third day, when they were sore, that two of the sons of Jacob, Simeon and Levi, Dinah's brethren, took each man his sword, and came upon the city boldly, and slew all the males.
Gen 49:7
Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce; and their wrath, for it was cruel: I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel.
corruption_summary: Some modern treatments romanticize Shechem's assault as a love story or recast the chapter chiefly through the lens of grievance, obscuring its moral lessons.
corruption_paragraphs: Attempts to soften the chapter into a tale of star-crossed love between Dinah and Shechem run against the plain word that he took her and defiled her by force; Scripture names it a folly wrought in Israel. Equally, readings that reduce the account to a single theme of victimhood eclipse the layered judgment the text renders upon every party—upon Shechem's sin, upon Jacob's passivity and worldly compromise, and upon the murderous treachery of Simeon and Levi, which the dying patriarch cursed.

The principle to recover is the holiness God requires of His covenant people and the evil of repaying wrong with greater wrong. The defilement was a real and grievous sin, and the brothers' vengeance was itself sin, deceitful and bloody. Vengeance belongs to the LORD, who alone judges righteously. The chapter calls Israel out from communion with the corrupt nations and casts every reader upon the need of redeeming grace, since sin festers even in the household of the promise.
roots_summary: The episode is rooted in the danger of Israel's mingling with Canaan and in the seriousness of sin within the covenant family.
roots_lines: Dinah was born to Jacob by Leah, listed among his children (Gen 30:21).
Her going out to see the daughters of the land exposed her to the heathen city.
Shechem's defilement provoked the deceitful covenant of circumcision (Gen 34:13-17).
Simeon and Levi's slaughter brought guilt and danger upon Jacob's house (Gen 34:30).
The deathbed prophecy cursed their cruelty and scattered them in Israel (Gen 49:7).
usage: The chapter is cited as a warning against unequal communion with the ungodly.
Simeon and Levi's deceit is the classic example of vengeance overstepping justice.
Jacob's rebuke is invoked to show the peril of compromise with surrounding nations.

etymology: Gershom (Hebrew Gershom) is explained in Scripture as "a stranger there," from ger (sojourner) and a word resembling "there," commemorating Moses' exile in Midian.
biblical_def: Gershom was the firstborn son of Moses by Zipporah the daughter of Jethro, born during the prophet's long sojourn in the land of Midian. The Scripture records that Moses named him Gershom, saying, I have been a stranger in a strange land. The name itself is a confession and a theme: it sets forth the pilgrim character of the people of God, who in this present world are sojourners and strangers, looking for a better country, that is, a heavenly. Moses, having fled the wrath of Pharaoh, dwelt as an exile keeping the flock of his father-in-law, and in the naming of his son he owned his estrangement from the land of promise even while the LORD was preparing him to deliver Israel. Gershom appears again in the line of the Levites, his descendants numbered among the sons of Levi, though the chief honor of the priesthood passed through Aaron. The strange episode at the inn, where the LORD sought to kill Moses and Zipporah circumcised her son, fixes the covenant sign upon the household even in the wilderness. So the brief notices of Gershom preach the pilgrim doctrine: the saints confess themselves strangers and sojourners, as were all the fathers, holding the things of this world loosely while they journey toward the rest that God has prepared.
webster_summary: The firstborn son of Moses, named to commemorate his father's exile, a standing emblem of the pilgrim life of God's people.
webster_full: GERSHOM, proper noun. From the Hebrew, "a stranger there"; the elder son of Moses by Zipporah.
Born in the land of Midian during Moses' flight from Pharaoh.
His name a perpetual confession of the sojourning estate of the godly.
As it is written, "And she bare him a son, and he called his name Gershom: for he said, I have been a stranger in a strange land" (Exo 2:22).
A figure of the pilgrim faith that seeks a better, heavenly country.
scriptures: Exo 2:22
And she bare him a son, and he called his name Gershom: for he said, I have been a stranger in a strange land.
Exo 18:3
And her two sons; of which the name of the one was Gershom; for he said, I have been an alien in a strange land:
The sons of Moses were, Gershom, and Eliezer.
Of the sons of Gershom, Shebuel was the chief.
corruption_summary: This name and its pilgrim theme face no postmodern redefinition, but the doctrine of the Christian as a stranger in the world is much neglected.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The biblical principle to recover is the pilgrim character of the people of God. In the naming of Gershom, Moses confessed himself a stranger in a strange land, and the New Testament takes up the same note when it calls the saints strangers and pilgrims who look for a city whose builder and maker is God. An age that prizes comfort and settledness easily forgets this estate.

To recover the lesson of Gershom is to hold the things of this world with a loose hand, knowing that here we have no continuing city. The patriarchs confessed they were strangers and sojourners; so must the believer. Yet the pilgrim is not homeless, for he journeys by faith toward the rest that remains for the people of God, sustained by the covenant sign sealed even in the wilderness.
roots_summary: The name is rooted in Moses' exile in Midian and in the wider scriptural theme of sojourning faith.
roots_lines: Moses fled to Midian after slaying the Egyptian (Exo 2:15).
He married Zipporah, daughter of the priest of Midian, who bore Gershom (Exo 2:21-22).
The name "stranger there" voiced Moses' estrangement from the land of promise.
At the inn the covenant sign of circumcision was laid upon the son (Exo 4:24-26).
Gershom's line is numbered among the Levites in the chronicles (1 Chr 23:15-16).
usage: Gershom's name is invoked to teach that believers are strangers in this world.
"A stranger in a strange land" has become a proverbial confession of exile.
The pilgrim theme links Gershom to Abraham and to the saints of Hebrews 11.

etymology: Barzillai (Hebrew Barzillay) means "man of iron," from barzel, iron; he was a wealthy Gileadite of Rogelim.
biblical_def: Barzillai the Gileadite was a very great and aged man who sustained King David in the hour of his flight, when Absalom had usurped the throne and the king passed over Jordan to Mahanaim. With Shobi and Machir, Barzillai brought beds, basins, and earthen vessels, with wheat, barley, flour, parched corn, beans, lentils, honey, butter, sheep, and cheese, that the king and his weary people might eat in the wilderness. This was no small loyalty, for to aid the rejected king when his cause seemed lost was to hazard all. When David was restored and would have brought Barzillai over Jordan to feed him in Jerusalem and reward his faithfulness with a place at the royal table, the old man, fourscore years of age, modestly declined, saying he could no longer discern good from evil nor taste what he ate and drank, and asked only to die in his own city by the grave of his father and mother. He sent Chimham his servant in his stead. Here is a portrait of faithful old age: liberal in giving, humble in receiving, content with little, and mindful of mortality and the grave. David remembered him to the last, charging Solomon to show kindness to the sons of Barzillai and let them be of those that eat at his table, for so he had stood by the king in his distress.
webster_summary: The aged and wealthy Gileadite who provisioned David in his flight from Absalom and humbly declined a place at the royal table.
webster_full: BARZILLAI, proper noun. From the Hebrew, "man of iron"; a great man of Gilead dwelling in Rogelim.
The host who supplied David and his people at Mahanaim in their distress.
An example of faithful, liberal, and self-effacing old age.
As it is written, "I am this day fourscore years old: and can I discern between good and evil?" (2 Sam 19:35).
Remembered by David to the last, who charged Solomon to show kindness to his sons.
scriptures: And it came to pass, when David was come to Mahanaim, that Shobi the son of Nahash of Rabbah of the children of Ammon, and Machir the son of Ammiel of Lodebar, and Barzillai the Gileadite of Rogelim,
Now Barzillai was a very aged man, even fourscore years old: and he had provided the king of sustenance while he lay at Mahanaim; for he was a very great man.

I am this day fourscore years old: and can I discern between good and evil? can thy servant taste what I eat or what I drink? can I hear any more the voice of singing men and singing women? wherefore then should thy servant be yet a burden unto my lord the king?
But shew kindness unto the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite, and let them be of those that eat at thy table: for so they came to me when I fled because of Absalom thy brother.
corruption_summary: Barzillai faces no postmodern redefinition, but his example of honored, generous, godly old age is much neglected in an age that prizes youth.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The biblical principle to recover is the honor and grace of faithful old age. Barzillai, fourscore years old, did not grasp at the comforts and dignities the king offered, but gave liberally in the day of trouble and asked only to die near the graves of his parents. An age that idolizes youth and dreads aging needs the steady iron faith of this Gileadite.

To recover Barzillai's example is to learn contentment, hospitality, and a sober mindfulness of death. He served the rejected king at great risk, sought no reward, and trusted his sons to the kindness of the crown. So the believer is taught to spend himself in love, to hold honors loosely, and to face the grave with the calm of one who has been faithful in his generation.
roots_summary: The account is rooted in the loyalty shown to David in the rebellion of Absalom and in the godly conduct of the aged.
roots_lines: Absalom's revolt drove David across Jordan to Mahanaim (2 Sam 17).
Barzillai, with Shobi and Machir, brought abundant provision to the king (2 Sam 17:27-29).
After the victory David offered Barzillai a place in Jerusalem (2 Sam 19:33).
The old man declined, sending Chimham in his stead (2 Sam 19:37-38).
David's dying charge to Solomon secured kindness for Barzillai's sons (1 Kgs 2:7).
usage: Barzillai is cited as the model of generous and self-forgetful old age.
His confession that he could no longer taste or hear is quoted on the frailties of age.
His name marks loyalty to the LORD's anointed in the day of adversity.

etymology: Araunah (Hebrew Aravnah; called Ornan in Chronicles) was a Jebusite of Jerusalem; the name is of Jebusite origin, possibly meaning "lord" or "noble."
biblical_def: Araunah the Jebusite, named Ornan in the Chronicles, owned the threshingfloor upon Mount Moriah where the plague that followed David's sinful numbering of the people was stayed. When the angel of the LORD stood between earth and heaven with a drawn sword over Jerusalem, the prophet Gad commanded David to rear an altar in the threshingfloor of Araunah. The Jebusite, seeing the king come, would have freely given the floor, the oxen for sacrifice, and the threshing instruments for wood; but David refused, saying, Nay, but I will surely buy it of thee at a price: neither will I offer burnt offerings unto the LORD my God of that which doth cost me nothing. So David bought the place and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver, and reared an altar, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and the LORD answered him and stayed the plague. This narrative is a true history of mercy after judgment, and it carries a great typology: the site of Araunah's floor became the very place where Solomon built the temple, the house of sacrifice for all Israel, and so the appointed place of atoning blood. David's confession—that worship which costs nothing is no worship—abides as a standing rebuke to cheap and careless religion, and the bought threshingfloor points forward to the costly sacrifice of Christ.
webster_summary: The Jebusite whose threshingfloor David bought for an altar, the site of the staying of the plague and of the future temple.
webster_full: ARAUNAH, proper noun. A Jebusite of Jerusalem, called Ornan in Chronicles; owner of the threshingfloor on Moriah.
The man from whom David purchased the place to build an altar to the LORD.
His threshingfloor became the site of Solomon's temple.
As it is written, "neither will I offer burnt offerings unto the LORD my God of that which doth cost me nothing" (2 Sam 24:24).
A type of the costly sacrifice required by God and fulfilled in Christ.
scriptures: And Gad came that day to David, and said unto him, Go up, rear an altar unto the LORD in the threshingfloor of Araunah the Jebusite.

And the king said unto Araunah, Nay; but I will surely buy it of thee at a price: neither will I offer burnt offerings unto the LORD my God of that which doth cost me nothing. So David bought the threshingfloor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver.
So David gave to Ornan for the place six hundred shekels of gold by weight.
Then David said, This is the house of the LORD God, and this is the altar of the burnt offering for Israel.
corruption_summary: Araunah faces no postmodern redefinition, but David's principle of costly worship is widely forgotten in an age of convenient religion.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The biblical principle to recover is that true worship costs the worshipper something. David refused to offer to the LORD that which cost him nothing, buying the threshingfloor and the oxen rather than accepting them as a gift. Cheap, careless, and convenient religion, which gives God the leftovers of time and treasure, stands rebuked by this Jebusite's floor.

The deeper lesson is the typology of the place itself. The threshingfloor where the plague was stayed became Mount Moriah, the site of the temple and its altar of burnt offering, the appointed place where atoning blood was shed for Israel. All of it pointed forward to the costly and once-for-all sacrifice of the Lord Jesus, who purchased His people not with silver and gold but with His own precious blood.
roots_summary: The account is rooted in David's sin of numbering Israel and in the mercy that appointed a place of sacrifice.
roots_lines: David's census of Israel brought a pestilence upon the land (2 Sam 24:15).
The angel of the LORD halted at the threshingfloor of Araunah (1 Chr 21:15).
Gad commanded David to build an altar in that place (2 Sam 24:18).
David bought the floor and oxen, refusing a free gift (2 Sam 24:24).
The site became Mount Moriah, where Solomon reared the temple (2 Chr 3:1).
usage: David's words on costly offering are quoted to rebuke careless worship.
Araunah's threshingfloor names the future temple mount, Mount Moriah.
The bought altar is read as a type of Christ's costly atonement.

etymology: Amalek (Hebrew Amaleq) was the grandson of Esau and the people descended from him; the name's meaning is uncertain, possibly "dweller in the valley" or "people that licks up."
biblical_def: Amalek was the grandson of Esau and the father of a fierce nomadic people who became the perpetual enemy of Israel. When Israel came forth from Egypt, Amalek fell upon them at Rephidim, smiting the feeble and the weary that lagged behind, and fearing not God. While Moses held up the rod of God upon the hill and Aaron and Hur stayed his hands, Joshua discomfited Amalek with the sword; and the LORD sware that He would have war with Amalek from generation to generation, and would utterly put out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven. Long after, the LORD commanded Saul through Samuel to smite Amalek and utterly destroy all that they had; but Saul spared Agag the king and the best of the spoil, and for this disobedience the kingdom was rent from him, while Samuel hewed Agag in pieces before the LORD. The history of Amalek is true and sobering: a nation under divine judgment for its unprovoked cruelty against the people of God. In the Reformed reading, Amalek stands also as a type of the flesh, that inveterate enemy which wars against the Spirit and which must be wholly mortified, not spared in part. As Saul's half-obedience was rebellion, so the believer learns that the flesh, like Agag, must not be pampered but put to death.
webster_summary: The nation descended from Esau's grandson, Israel's perpetual foe under divine judgment, and a type of the warring flesh.
webster_full: AMALEK, proper noun. From the Hebrew Amaleq; grandson of Esau and the people sprung from him.
The first nation to make war on Israel after the Exodus, at Rephidim.
A people devoted to destruction by the perpetual decree of the LORD.
As it is written, "the LORD hath sworn that the LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation" (Exo 17:16).
In figure, the unmortified flesh that wars against the Spirit and must be wholly slain.
scriptures: And it came to pass, when Moses held up his hand, that Israel prevailed: and when he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed.
For he said, Because the LORD hath sworn that the LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation.
Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass.
For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry. Because thou hast rejected the word of the LORD, he hath also rejected thee from being king.
corruption_summary: The command to destroy Amalek is a favorite object of modern moral objection, charged as cruelty unworthy of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern objectors frequently brandish the war against Amalek as proof of a harsh or unjust deity, divorcing the command from its righteous ground. But Scripture grounds the judgment in Amalek's own unprovoked cruelty—falling upon the feeble and weary, and fearing not God—and in the LORD's sovereign right to judge nations in His own time and measure. The Judge of all the earth does right. Amalek had filled up the measure of its iniquity, and the destruction was a holy and just sentence, not arbitrary violence.

The principle to recover is twofold. First, the holiness and justice of God, who hates sin and will by no means clear the guilty, yet who is longsuffering for centuries before judgment falls. Second, the spiritual application drawn out by the saints: Amalek figures the flesh, that bitter enemy of the soul. Saul's sparing of Agag and the best of the spoil was disobedience counted as rebellion; so the believer must not spare any darling lust but mortify the flesh wholly, for to spare it is to rebel against the word of the LORD.
roots_summary: The enmity is rooted in Amalek's unprovoked attack on Israel and in the LORD's sworn and perpetual judgment.
roots_lines: Amalek descended from Esau through Eliphaz (Gen 36:12).
The attack at Rephidim provoked the LORD's oath of perpetual war (Exo 17:8-16).
Moses charged Israel to remember and blot out Amalek (Deut 25:17-19).
Saul's partial obedience against Agag cost him the kingdom (1 Sam 15).
Agag's sparing and Samuel's judgment teach the mortifying of the flesh.
usage: Amalek is the standing emblem of Israel's implacable enemy.
"Sparing Agag" names the sin of leaving any lust unmortified.
The lifted hands of Moses are cited as a picture of prevailing prayer in battle.

etymology: Adam (Hebrew Adam) means "man" and is connected with adamah, the ground from which he was formed; the proper name of the first man.
biblical_def: Adam was the first man, formed by God of the dust of the ground, into whose nostrils the LORD breathed the breath of life so that he became a living soul. Created in the image of God, male and female, given dominion over the creatures and set in the garden of Eden, Adam was constituted not merely the first of the race but its federal head and representative. To him God gave the covenant of works, with the tree of the knowledge of good and evil as its test; and when Adam ate, he sinned not for himself alone but for all his posterity descending from him by ordinary generation. As the apostle teaches, by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin, and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned. Thus the guilt of Adam's first transgression is imputed to his seed, and a corrupt nature conveyed to them, the original sin of the whole race. Yet Adam is set forth in Scripture as the figure of Him that was to come, for as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive. The first Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam, the Lord Jesus Christ, a quickening spirit. So the federal headship of Adam unto condemnation is answered by the federal headship of Christ unto justification and life, the very hinge of the gospel.
webster_summary: The first man and federal head of the human race, by whose disobedience sin and death came upon all, set forth as the figure of Christ the last Adam.
webster_full: ADAM, proper noun. From the Hebrew for "man," akin to adamah, ground; the first man, formed of the dust.
Created in the image of God and made the federal head of his posterity.
By his first transgression sin and death entered the world and passed upon all men.
As it is written, "For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive" (1 Cor 15:22).
A figure of Him that was to come, answered by Christ the last Adam, a quickening spirit.
scriptures: Gen 2:7
And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
Rom 5:12
Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned:
For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.
And so it is written, The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit.
corruption_summary: The historicity of Adam is widely denied today, his fall reduced to myth and his federal headship dismissed, undermining the gospel itself.
corruption_paragraphs: The chief assault on Adam in our day is the denial that he ever lived—the reduction of the first man to a symbol, an archetype, or a poetic figure standing for humanity in general rather than a real individual created by God at the beginning. This is no minor revision. If there was no historical Adam who really sinned, then there is no real imputation of guilt, no original sin transmitted to the race, and the apostle's argument in Romans 5 and First Corinthians 15 collapses. Paul reasons from a true and historical Adam to a true and historical Christ; deny the one and you wound the other.

The principle to recover is the federal headship of Adam and the parallel headship of Christ, which together form the architecture of the gospel. Adam was constituted the covenant representative of all his natural posterity, so that his fall is our fall and his guilt our guilt. Against this stands the last Adam, the Lord Jesus, whose obedience and sacrifice are imputed to all who are in Him by faith. As in Adam all die, so in Christ shall all His people be made alive. To hold fast the historical Adam is to hold fast salvation by imputed righteousness.
roots_summary: The doctrine is rooted in the creation and fall of Genesis and in the apostolic parallel of the two Adams.
roots_lines: Adam was formed of the dust and made a living soul (Gen 2:7).
He was placed under the covenant of works in Eden (Gen 2:16-17).
His transgression brought sin and death upon all his posterity (Rom 5:12).
His guilt and corruption are imputed and conveyed to the race as original sin.
Christ the last Adam answers the first as the head of a redeemed humanity (1 Cor 15:45).
usage: "In Adam" names the whole race under condemnation by his fall.
"The last Adam" is a title of Christ as the new covenant head.
The two Adams frame the Reformed doctrine of imputation and federal headship.

etymology: Machpelah (Hebrew Makhpelah) means "double" or "doubled," perhaps from the cave's twofold chamber; the field and cave near Mamre at Hebron.
biblical_def: The cave of Machpelah was the burying place of the patriarchs, the field and cave that Abraham bought of Ephron the Hittite for a possession of a buryingplace, when Sarah died at Kirjath-arba, which is Hebron, in the land of Canaan. Though God had promised Abraham the whole land, in his lifetime he possessed not so much as to set his foot on, save this one field, which he purchased openly before the sons of Heth for four hundred shekels of silver, current money with the merchant. He would not take it as a gift but bought it outright, that he might have a sure title in the land of promise. There Abraham buried Sarah; there afterward Abraham himself was buried, and Isaac and Rebekah, and Leah, and Jacob, whose body Joseph and his brethren carried up out of Egypt to lay in the cave with his fathers. The purchase of Machpelah is a true history and a great act of faith: by securing a grave in Canaan, the patriarchs confessed that they believed the promise of the land, and that they looked beyond their own deaths to the resurrection and the inheritance God had sworn. They died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off and embraced them, confessing they were strangers and pilgrims, and so the cave became a standing pledge of the covenant and a witness to the hope of resurrection.
webster_summary: The field and cave at Hebron that Abraham bought for a burying place, where the patriarchs and their wives were laid in hope of the promise.
webster_full: CAVE OF MACHPELAH, proper noun. From the Hebrew Makhpelah, "double"; the field and cave near Mamre at Hebron.
Purchased by Abraham of Ephron the Hittite as a possession of a buryingplace.
The resting place of Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, Leah, and Jacob.
As it is written, "the field, and the cave that is therein, were made sure unto Abraham for a possession of a buryingplace by the sons of Heth" (Gen 23:20).
A pledge of faith in the promise of the land and the hope of resurrection.
scriptures: Gen 23:9
That he may give me the cave of Machpelah, which he hath, which is in the end of his field; for as much money as it is worth he shall give it me for a possession of a buryingplace amongst you.
And after this, Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the cave of the field of Machpelah before Mamre: the same is Hebron in the land of Canaan.
And the field, and the cave that is therein, were made sure unto Abraham for a possession of a buryingplace by the sons of Heth.
There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife; there they buried Isaac and Rebekah his wife; and there I buried Leah.
corruption_summary: Machpelah faces no postmodern redefinition, but the patriarchs' faith in the promise and the resurrection is too little pondered.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The biblical principle to recover is the patriarchal faith that bought a grave in Canaan as a pledge of God's promise. Abraham, owning no more of the promised land than this one field, paid full price for it rather than receive it as a gift, that he might hold a sure title and so confess his faith that his seed would inherit the whole. He died in faith, not having received the promise, but having seen it afar off.

The deeper lesson is the hope of resurrection. The patriarchs were laid in Machpelah not as men without hope but as those who believed God would keep covenant with them and their seed and raise them up at the last. To purchase a burying place in the land of promise was to plant a stake of faith in the soil of God's word. So the cave teaches the believer to face death as a sojourner who waits, sure of the inheritance reserved in heaven and of the resurrection of the body.
roots_summary: The purchase is rooted in the Abrahamic covenant of the land and in the patriarchs' faith in the resurrection.
roots_lines: God had promised the land of Canaan to Abraham and his seed (Gen 13:15).
Sarah's death at Hebron occasioned the purchase of the burying place (Gen 23:2).
Abraham bought field and cave of Ephron for four hundred shekels (Gen 23:16).
Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and their wives were buried there (Gen 49:31).
Jacob's body was carried from Egypt to rest with his fathers (Gen 50:13).
usage: Machpelah is cited as the one foothold Abraham held in the promised land.
The purchase is read as an act of faith in the covenant of the land.
The patriarchs' graves are invoked as witnesses to the hope of resurrection.
